ACTIONS ARTIFACT POISONING CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Can a fork PR's artifact get executed by your privileged workflow?

A job triggered by workflow_run runs with your repository's full GITHUB_TOKEN and secrets, even though the run it reacts to was raised by a stranger's fork. GitHub's own Actions Security Lab, and independent research from Wiz, Legit Security and Orca Security, document the resulting attack as "artifact poisoning": the fork-triggered workflow uploads an artifact, your privileged handler downloads it, and if it executes anything from that artifact, the fork gets code execution in your context. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds both a downloaded artifact that gets executed later in the same job, and a download step with no name: pin, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Common questions

What is GitHub Actions artifact poisoning?

A workflow triggered by workflow_run runs with the base repository's full GITHUB_TOKEN and secrets, even though the run it reacts to — typically a pull_request build or test workflow — was raised by a stranger's fork. GitHub's own Actions Security Lab, and independent research from Wiz, Legit Security and Orca Security, document artifact poisoning as the resulting attack: the fork-triggered workflow uploads an artifact, the privileged workflow_run handler downloads it, and if that handler executes anything from the downloaded content, the fork gets code execution in the privileged context.

How is this different from the pwn-request or cache-poisoning patterns?

Same trigger gate — a job reachable from an untrusted fork that a privileged workflow later trusts — applied to a third sink. Actions Injection Check flags checking out an untrusted git ref or interpolating an untrusted event expression into a shell command. Actions Cache Poisoning Check flags a fork-writable Actions cache entry a privileged workflow later restores. This flags a downloaded artifact's file contents being executed, or an artifact download with no name: pin.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my workflow_run jobs are safe?

No. This checks two specific, narrow patterns in a single workflow file at a time. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your repository's overall security. It assumes a workflow_run download is reading the triggering run's own artifacts, and it does not inspect what an action called by uses: does internally with a downloaded path.

Why is an unscoped download flagged even with no execution nearby?

A download-artifact step with no name: input pulls in every artifact the fork-controlled triggering run uploaded, not one specific, expected one. That widens what untrusted content enters the privileged job even if nothing in this file executes it directly — a later step, or a called action, might still read it.

More: what is GitHub Actions artifact poisoning? See also this checker vs. reading the workflow YAML by hand.

vs-reading-the-workflow-yaml-by-hand.htm.text:
← Actions Artifact Poisoning Check

Actions Artifact Poisoning Check vs. reading the workflow YAML by hand

This page names no company or product — reading a workflow file before trusting it is a habit most maintainers already have, not a competing tool. The gap is not carelessness: the vulnerable pattern this checker looks for is a relationship between two steps that can sit many lines apart, neither one suspicious on its own.

What a manual read catches reliably

An obviously dangerous single line — a run: step that pipes curl output straight into bash, or a trigger that looks wrong on its face. Those stand out to a reviewer scanning top to bottom, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

What a manual read struggles with, and why

Where the two diverge on this specific pattern.
CaseReading by handThis checker
A download-artifact step and the run step that later executes its contentsCan sit many unrelated-looking steps apart in the same job; neither line looks suspicious read on its ownTracks the download across every subsequent step in the job body and flags the pair together, with both line numbers
The workflow_run trigger's significanceEasy to read past, especially listed alongside other triggers on one line -- its meaning here is about who controls the artifact's bytes, not the keyword itselfChecks for the trigger explicitly before treating a download-and-execute pair as a finding, so the connection is made whether or not a reader consciously registered the trigger
A download-artifact step with no name: inputAn absence, not a suspicious presence -- there is no unusual text to catch a reader's eye, only a missing oneFlags every download-artifact step with no name: regardless of what else looks ordinary around it
Whether execution "looks like" executionchmod +x, ./script, bash, source, python, node, and eval all read as ordinary build or test commands out of contextMatches the same execution-shaped patterns specifically in a run step that follows a download in the same job, not in isolation

None of this is about attention or diligence. The finding lives in a relationship between two steps, not in either step alone -- which is exactly the shape of thing a linear read is worst at holding onto across a long job body.

Run the free artifact poisoning check

When to still read the file yourself

This tool looks for exactly two patterns: a workflow_run job that downloads an artifact and later runs something that looks like execution, and an unscoped download-artifact step. It reports only those. It does not evaluate anything else in the workflow, does not know whether a matched run: step is actually dangerous in context versus a false positive, and makes no network call to check anything beyond the pasted text. Judging the surrounding job logic, and everything outside these two patterns, is still a job for reading the workflow yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a workflow file by hand catch reliably?

An obviously dangerous single line: a run: step that pipes curl output straight into bash, or a workflow trigger that looks wrong on its face. Those stand out to a reviewer scanning a file top to bottom, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

Why is the artifact-poisoning pattern specifically hard to catch by reading?

Because the two halves of it are rarely adjacent. A download-artifact step usually appears early in a job to fetch build output; the step that executes something from disk -- a chmod +x, a ./script.sh, a bash some-file -- can appear many steps later, often looking like an unrelated build or test step on its own. Neither line is suspicious in isolation. The finding only exists in the relationship between the two, which requires holding the fact that this job downloaded a fork-influenced artifact in mind while reading every subsequent step until one of them executes something.

Why does the workflow_run trigger matter, and is it obvious from the file?

workflow_run is what makes the downloaded artifact's contents attacker-influenced in the first place: the job runs with the base repository's permissions and secrets, but the artifact it downloads was uploaded by the fork-triggered run this workflow reacts to. The trigger line itself is easy to read past, especially in a file with several triggers listed together (push, pull_request, workflow_run on one line) -- and its significance here is not that the keyword appears, but that it changes who controls the bytes a later step in the same job might execute.

Is a download-artifact step with no name: input an obvious problem to spot?

No -- it is the absence of something, which is much harder to notice while reading than a suspicious line would be. A download-artifact step with no name: pulls in every artifact the triggering run uploaded rather than one specific, expected one, widening what untrusted content enters the job. There is no unusual-looking text to catch a reader's eye; the step simply omits an input, and confirming that requires already knowing to check for it on every such step in every workflow.

Does a clean scan from this tool mean my workflow has no security issues?

No. This tool looks for exactly two patterns -- a workflow_run job that downloads an artifact and later runs something that looks like execution, and an unscoped download-artifact step -- and reports only those. A clean result means neither pattern was found in the pasted text; it says nothing about any other risk in the workflow, and it is not a security audit.

vs-zizmor.html.text:
← Actions Artifact Poisoning Check

Actions Artifact Poisoning Check vs. zizmor

zizmor audits a GitHub Actions workflow against 41 checks, per its own documentation, but none of them looks at what a workflow_run job does with a downloaded artifact. Its dangerous-triggers audit flags workflow_run itself, by its mere presence, on every job that uses it. Its artipacked audit checks the opposite direction of an artifact pipeline -- credentials leaking out through an upload, not a download's contents getting executed. This page checks the specific behavior neither of those covers, free, on one pasted file, with nothing to install.

What each tool is for

zizmor (github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions, installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor and run against workflow files or a whole repository. Per its own documentation it ships 41 audits covering unpinned or typosquatted uses: references, excessive permission scopes, template injection, impostor commits, and more, and can emit SARIF for GitHub code scanning. Two of its audits sit near this page's territory without covering it: dangerous-triggers flags pull_request_target and workflow_run as fundamentally hard to use safely, by the trigger's presence alone; artipacked flags actions/checkout persisting a credential that a later upload-artifact step might publish. Neither inspects what a workflow_run job does with something it downloads.

This checker does exactly that and nothing else: paste the YAML of a workflow file, and it finds every workflow_run job that downloads an artifact (actions/download-artifact or dawidd6/action-download-artifact) and later runs something that looks like it executes a file from disk, plus every download-artifact step with no name: input. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install and no token, and makes no network call of its own under any configuration.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want one maintained scanner covering a broad catalogue of GitHub Actions security patterns.zizmor -- 41 audits is its entire job, and this tool checks one narrow pattern none of them covers.
My workflow already trips zizmor's dangerous-triggers finding on a workflow_run job -- is this specific job the dangerous one?This checker -- it reads what the job actually does with a download, rather than flagging the trigger's presence alone.
I want to know if a credential could leak out through an artifact my workflow uploads.zizmor's artipacked audit -- that is the upload side of the pipeline, which this tool does not check.
I want to know if a downloaded artifact could get executed, or is pulled in unscoped, in a privileged workflow_run job.This checker -- paste the YAML, get the two-row answer, no CLI and no repository access.
I want SARIF output wired into GitHub code scanning, or a report across an entire repository of workflows.zizmor -- its CLI and GitHub Action are built for exactly that.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run zizmor in CI for its full catalogue and still reach for this page the moment the question is specifically "does this workflow_run job download and execute an artifact" -- a question zizmor's own audit list, read closely, does not currently answer.

Run the free artifact poisoning check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or zizmor?

Both, for different questions. zizmor is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis CLI (installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor) that audits a GitHub Actions workflow, or a whole repository of them, against 41 checks per its own documentation -- unpinned actions, excessive permissions, credential leakage, impostor commits, template injection, and more, with SARIF output for GitHub code scanning. None of those 41 is the specific pattern this page checks: a workflow_run job that downloads an artifact and later executes something from it, or a download-artifact step with no name: pin. If you want one maintained tool covering a broad catalogue of GitHub Actions security patterns, run zizmor. If you want to know whether the one workflow_run job in front of you actually does something dangerous with a downloaded artifact, this page answers that specifically, with nothing to install.

Does zizmor already catch what this tool catches?

Not the same finding. zizmor's dangerous-triggers audit flags workflow_run by its mere presence in a workflow -- per its own documentation it is one of the trigger types the audit treats as fundamentally dangerous, and it fires on every workflow that uses the trigger at all, regardless of what the job actually does. zizmor's artipacked audit checks the opposite direction of an artifact pipeline: a credential persisted by actions/checkout leaking out through an uploaded artifact, not a downloaded artifact's contents being executed. Neither audit inspects what a workflow_run job does with something it downloads. This page fills that specific gap: it flags only a downloaded artifact getting executed later in the same job, or a download-artifact step with no name: input, and says nothing about a workflow_run job that does neither.

Why check something zizmor's broader trigger audit already flags?

Because zizmor's signal there is coarse on purpose: dangerous-triggers exists to warn that pull_request_target and workflow_run are hard to use safely at all, not to say which specific job behavior makes one unsafe. A workflow_run job that never touches an artifact, and one that downloads and executes a fork-controlled artifact, both trip the same zizmor finding with the same severity. This page reads what the job actually does with a download and reports only the two behaviors that make it dangerous, so a maintainer already carrying a dangerous-triggers finding can tell whether this specific job is the one that needs fixing first.

Does this tool need a GitHub token or repository access the way some zizmor audits do?

No, never. zizmor documents an optional online mode -- enabled by setting GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN -- that some of its audits use for checks needing GitHub API access, such as confirming a pinned commit is genuinely reachable from the repository. This page has no online mode to opt into and no repository access at all: you paste the YAML, and the scan runs entirely in this browser tab with no network call of its own under any configuration.

Is this page affiliated with zizmor or its maintainers?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by zizmor, zizmorcore, or its maintainers. zizmor is an independent open-source project, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation and source repository at github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor.

what-is-github-actions-artifact-poisonin.text:
← Actions Artifact Poisoning Check

What is GitHub Actions artifact poisoning?

workflow_run is a trigger that fires when a separate workflow run completes — commonly used so a privileged workflow can react to an unprivileged pull_request build without inheriting the fork's ability to change what that workflow does by editing the workflow file itself. The workflow_run job runs in the context of the base repository, with the base repository's GITHUB_TOKEN and secrets — but the run it reacts to was still triggered by whoever opened the pull request, who might be a stranger.

That is a deliberate, documented design, and it is safe on its own. The risk is what the privileged job does with the artifact the unprivileged run produced:

on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [build-pr]
    types: [completed]
jobs:
  publish-results:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
      - run: |
          chmod +x ./test-results/publish.sh
          ./test-results/publish.sh

The artifact was uploaded by the fork-triggered build-pr workflow, so its contents — not just the event payload GitHub itself controls — are whatever the fork put there. Downloading it is not the risk; running it is. GitHub's own Actions Security Lab, and independent research from Wiz, Legit Security and Orca Security, document this pattern as "artifact poisoning": a fork can put a script in the artifact it uploads and rely on the privileged handler to execute it unchecked.

A second, quieter version

A download-artifact step with no name: input pulls in every artifact the triggering run uploaded, not one specific, expected one. Even if nothing in the same job executes anything directly, that widens what untrusted content is sitting on disk for a later step, or an action called by uses:, to pick up.

The fix

  • Never execute, source, or eval anything read from a downloaded artifact. Treat it as data: read specific, expected fields and validate their shape before use.
  • If the privileged job genuinely needs the fork's build output, keep the build itself unprivileged (plain pull_request, no secrets) and have the privileged job read only reviewed, structured results — not executable content.
  • Pin name: on every download-artifact step so it fetches exactly the artifact you expect, not everything the triggering run happened to upload.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Artifact Poisoning Check to find every workflow_run job that downloads and later executes an artifact, and every unscoped download, across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow has either pattern — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is safe — only that these two documented patterns were not found.
